Action Plan:
1. Provide prescription for a stronger non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicine (exact agent/dose/route/frequency not documented) to be taken with food; advise concurrent use of paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented) if required for pain control.  
2. Arrange an urgent face-to-face appointment through the support team for full neurological examination, fundoscopy and blood pressure measurement.  
3. If examination supports migraine with aura, review suitability of the current combined oral contraceptive pill and discuss alternative contraception.  
4. Educate patient on red-flag symptoms (sudden escalation of pain, new neurological deficit, uncontrollable vomiting, visual loss); instruct to attend Emergency Department (A&E) immediately if these occur.  
5. Safety-net: cancel in-person appointment if headache completely resolves before the visit; otherwise attend as planned.  
6. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• 32-year-old female (name/DOB/address verbally confirmed) presents with a “blinding” headache for 3 days.  
  – Onset: Sudden upon waking three days ago.  
  – Duration/Progression: Constant; partially improves with ibuprofen yet never fully resolves.  
  – Location: Diffuse, worst over right eye.  
  – Severity: 8/10 at worst; falls to ~5/10 with ibuprofen.  
  – Character/Associated: Photophobia, transient “shooting lights” (visual disturbance), mild nausea (no vomiting).  
  – Aggravating: Bright light, sudden standing, rapid head movement.  
  – Relieving: Ibuprofen (partial), sleep; headache does not wake her at night.  
  – No focal weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, fever, sinus symptoms, neck stiffness, smell/taste change.  
• Past headaches: Mild, short-lived episodes responsive to ibuprofen; never lasted >2 days.  
• Past medical history: None significant. Childhood “pain” of unclear nature resolved.  
• Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill (brand not specified; started 1 yr ago); ibuprofen PRN for pain.  
• Allergies: None known.  
• Family history: Mother suffers from migraines with vomiting.  
• Social: Lives alone; works from home; non-smoker; alcohol ≈3 drinks once weekly; no recreational drugs; no recent travel.  
• Review of systems otherwise non-contributory.

Objective:
• Tele-consultation; no physical examination performed.  
• Afebrile by history.  
• No vital signs or neurological / ocular examination findings available.  
• No investigations performed to date.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Severe persistent headache (3 days):
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Migraine with visual aura (DDx: “Migraine with visual aura” – High).  
   – Differential diagnosis:
     • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (Medium) – risk factor: estrogen OCP; positional component.  
     • Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Medium) – young female, visual disturbance.  
     • Tension-type headache (Low-Medium) – diffuse pain but photophobia/visual aura argue against.  
     • Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Low) – sudden severe onset but lacks thunderclap pattern and meningism.  
   – Investigations planned: In-person neurological examination, fundoscopy for papilledema/optic changes, blood pressure; further imaging (MRI/MRV, CT, lumbar puncture) to be considered if red flags or examination abnormal.  
   – Treatment planned: Prescribe stronger NSAID (agent/dose/route/frequency not documented) and allow concurrent paracetamol; advise taking with food.  
   – Relevant referrals: None at present; will escalate/referral to neurology or emergency care if examination or course indicates.

2. Combined oral contraceptive pill review:
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Need to reassess suitability of estrogen-containing OCP if migraine with aura confirmed.  
   – Differential diagnosis: OCP-induced migraine (DDx category “OCP-related migraine”).  
   – Investigations planned: Blood pressure measurement at upcoming appointment.  
   – Treatment planned: Continue current pill until review; discuss alternative contraception if aura-positive migraine diagnosed.  
   – Relevant referrals: Family planning clinic if pill change required.

3. Safety-netting / escalation plan:
   – Assessment: Risk of potential serious secondary headache disorders (e.g., CVST, SAH).  
   – Plan: Patient instructed to attend Emergency Department if headache intensifies, changes character, new neurological symptoms develop, or becomes unbearable.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: No vital signs, fundoscopy, neurological examination, or imaging obtained during tele-visit; medication names and exact dosing for new analgesic not documented.  
● Internal conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Mostly clear; brief instances of inaudible patient name and pill brand.
